The Defence brief asserts that because the commission members allegedly never implemented their task, it shows -- somehow shows Stojic's lack of authority over prison matters. Not correct. First, the fact that Stojic could and did order the formation of this commission plainly indicates that he did have power to act, as we've just been discussing. And further, it is not true that the establishment of this commission did not serve its purpose. For its appointed president, Berislav Pusic, this function expanded his own role with respect to prisoners and further confirmed his key place in the JCE 2 and JCE 1 involving the camps and the deportation of Muslims from the camps. Those may be functions which Mr. Stojic is not anxious to embrace, but he cannot pretend that they didn't exist. In direct reference to Stojic's order establishing the commission, Pusic confirmed his de jure responsibilities over the HVO prisoners and over the HVO personnel who held them, implementing Stojic's directive to assemble information about the detainees, the conditions and circumstances of their confinement, and their classification and potential release. You can see that as P04141. Mr. Stojic next turns to say, well, it was actually the military Judges who were responsible for the prisoners held at the HVO facilities. That may be true, at least to the extent of only those soldiers who were specifically being held on the order of an HVO military judge. The Prosecution submits that those were pretty few and far between. These are not the prisoners of war. These are not the detained Muslim men, for the most part, that we're talking about. So even taking as -- even taking arguendo that that may be true, the fact that a military judge may have had some responsibility as some few of the detainees in HVO prisons and facilities does not let Mr. Stojic off the hook. In fact, one of the issues in this case concerning the detained individuals was a lack of classification. People didn't know and the HVO didn't know. Are they civilians? Are they prisoners of war? Are they detained HVO members? Why are they being held? What categories are they in? How are they classified? That was indeed one of the very core problems that directly relates to this particular issue. What is perhaps most important about the military judge situation in which the report from the military judge, which Stojic cites as P06520, is that it indicates as to who was responsible for the operation of the Ljubuski prison because who does this military judge send his report to? Three people: The head of the government, Mr. Prlic; the head of the Defence Department, Mr. Stojic; and the head of Military Police Administration, Mr. Coric. That's who that military judge thought was responsible. Stojic and the military police. The Prosecution persists in its position that Stojic had substantial responsibility for the HVO military police as set out in our final brief. In his final brief, Stojic does not seem to seriously contest this connection, but again dismisses what he claims were, quote, "only administrative and logistical responsibilities." While the Prosecution submits that Stojic's role and involvements concerning the military police was, in fact, much more than he let's on, we nonetheless reject again any notion or any premise that, quote, "mere or only administrative responsibilities or functions is somehow insufficient for purposes of criminal liability or contribution to a joint criminal enterprise." As to humanitarian aid, finally in about -- excuse me, in the connection of blocking or manipulation of humanitarian aid, the Stojic position on this seems to be another instance where the accused claims the power only to do good but no power to do ill. While he claims to have no role or responsibility bearing on the movement, distribution, or receipt of humanitarian aid, he nonetheless seeks credit for giving permission or arranging for medical supplies to reach the East Mostar war hospital. Excuse me one moment, Your Honours. My apologies. I want to turn, last two topics for me, and one is the pointing the finger, if you will, at other persons or other institutions in terms of, if I can call it, blame shifting. It wasn't me. I didn't have power. I didn't have responsibility. I didn't have authority. It was someone else. Various of the accused point the finger at someone or something else as the person or institution with the, quote, "real power" or the person or institution that was really responsible or really to blame. Putting aside for now the instances where they point the finger at each other, here are some of the other persons or institutions which are routinely blamed, if you will: Well, of course, perhaps the number one is Boban. The Prosecution has never denied, does not deny today, that Boban was the president of Herceg-Bosna and at least on paper, at least de jure, the supreme commander of the HVO military. In connection with the Defence pointing at the famous empty chair of the courtroom or empty chairs, perhaps to Boban in particular, perhaps others that are not here in court, I would note what Robert Jackson said in his closing at Nuremberg concerning a certain person or persons who were missing from that trial, Jackson: "I shall not dissent from this consensus, nor do I deny that all these dead and missing men share the guilt. In crimes so reprehensible that degrees of guilt have lost their significance, they may have played the most evil parts, but their quilt cannot exculpate the defendants. Hitler did not carry all responsibility to the grave with him. All the guilt is not wrapped in Himmler's shroud. It these dead men whom these living chose to be their partners in this great conspiratorial brotherhood, and the crimes that they did together they must pay for one by one." Having said that, let's consider Boban's role and its relation to the evidence in this case. First, even assuming that Boban had significant power, he could not have run Herceg-Bosna and the HVO all by himself. He could not and did not run the government. Prlic did. He could not and did not run the HVO Department of Defence. Stojic did. He could not and did not run the HVO Main Staff. Praljak and Petkovic did. He did not run the HVO military police. Coric did. He did not run the service for exchange of prisoners and other persons. Pusic did. Second, even if Boban was a significant player, and surely he was, surely he was -- you've heard the evidence over the last day and a half already of Boban's role, and again the Prosecution has never denied that, but even if he was a significant player, he was a leadership member of the same joint criminal enterprise so that his acts and behaviour are linked with and attributable to the other members of the joint criminal enterprise, including the accused. Assuming arguendo that Boban played a significant role in the joint criminal enterprise, that does not negate or diminish the liability of the various accused. As Jackson said, they must be held responsible for their crimes one by one. The accused were members of the same JCE and are liable for every crime committed in pursuit of the common purpose provided that the crime can be imputed to a JCE member. So pointing the finger at Boban, unless there is something very specific that somehow disconnects him from the joint criminal enterprise, pointing the finger at Boban does not really get them very far. Third, there is no evidence that Boban was a hands-on administrator as either president, that is head of state, not head of government because that was Mr. Prlic's role, or as supreme commander. The Stojic Defence expert witness Davor Marijan hit the nail on the head, and I made reference to this earlier: "Practically from the summer of 1992, we have no evidence that Mr. Boban commanded the armed forces, which means he had delegated his powers." Transcript 35866. Not a Prosecution witness, Defence expert. There is no evidence. We have no evidence that Mr. Boban commanded the armed forces. Number four, throughout the Croat-Muslim conflict Boban spent much if not most of his time abroad representing the HVO and the Bosnian Croats in international peace negotiations and talks outside Bosnia in such places as Zagreb, Geneva, and New York without having much knowledge of many of the day-to-day military operations in the field. The Chamber has seen and heard evidence after evidence of his extensive involvement in those sorts of activities. Your Honour, again, out of an abundance of caution I'd ask to go briefly into private session on some private-session testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Next, Neven Tomic, Prlic Defence witness, was asked this: "How often was Mr. Boban, in your experience, how often was Mr. Boban himself actually in Mostar during this time? And I mean we're roughly talking mid-1992 until the end of 1993, about an 18-month period. I mean, you may have had an office, but perhaps you will tell us he was never there or perhaps he was there every day. "A. He would come very seldom. He spent most of his time in Grude." Number seven, the accused Slobodan Praljak: "For instance, you remember that convoy in Citluk. So it was the civilians that stopped the convoy. For the convoy to go through, one should first talk to the civilians and the person to do that should have been Mate Boban. So that was a political issue. But Mate Boban fails to appear for the talks, so Dr. Jadranko Prlic addresses the crowd." Once again, Boban's a no-show. It falls to Mr. Prlic to actually do the work. I suggest, and respectfully submit to the Chamber that that was true most of the time. As I mentioned previously, Davor Marijan made it very clear, quote, "... practically from the summer of 1992, we have no evidence that Mr. Boban commanded the armed forces." Davor Marijan again: "It's a fact, and at least I didn't see it, we have very few documents from Mr. Boban in 1993. I wonder if there are any, in fact. There was a document about the establishment of a military district, but not appointments, so obviously some powers have been transferred from him, which doesn't mean that he did not remain the supreme commander." In name, I suppose. That's Boban. Another organisation or entity that some of the accused like to point as well that was the real power and the responsibility was the HZ-HB Presidency, the legislative body. Yes, that body did officially exist de jure, and yes it did meet on some occasions, but there are two fundamental problems with this being -- with that body being, if you will, the fall-guy. First, this was a legislative body, not an executive government or administrative authority. Whatever laws or policies it might have made, it was not the body which administered, executed, or carried out those laws and policies. Executing Herceg-Bosna law and policy was first and foremost the responsibility of the Prlic government, and Prlic, as we saw earlier, was personally and individually responsible for the work of his government. Second, and perhaps more importantly, the HZ -- HZ-HB Presidency was not in session during the period from 17 October 1992, to 28 August 1993. Not functioning, not meeting. During that time, as I mentioned earlier today, it had delegated its full legislative powers to the Prlic government. They weren't meeting. They weren't in session. They weren't a factor. Accordingly, during the core period of the indictment, from October 1992 to at least the end of August 1993, Prlic's HVO government again was the highest, most powerful body in Herceg-Bosna combining supreme, executive, legislative, and administrative powers in that government. Indeed, the HVO's -- HVO government's own report for the year 1992, it's year-end report, summarised and fully confirmed its expanded powers, saying that, quote, "responsibility for determining policies in all spheres," in all spheres, "have been transferred to the Prlic government." And that can be found at P00128. The Defence witness Zoran Buntic, as I mentioned earlier today but I'll briefly mention again in this specific context, made it clear and testified, "The HVO HZ-HB was the highest executive and controlling body. That is beyond dispute." His words, not mine. One or more of the accused from time to time have pointed the finger at the HDZ-BiH party. We talked about that yesterday. The party was not functioning. The party was frozen. The party was not a factor. Another frequent target, someone else that the finger was pointed at, were the HVO municipal authorities. We talked about that earlier today. Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Filipovic, and others clearly said unequivocally those bodies did not control, did not issue orders, did not direct the HVO military. No one can point the finger at the HVO municipal authorities and say they were responsible. They did not issue the orders or give the direction. The final topic for me at this point is -- that I want to close with is this point, and that is that despite all the claims of no power, no authority, no ability to act, the evidence is clear that the HVO and these accused could take strong and forceful action when they really wanted to. The accused have generally claimed to have had no power or ability to act, but the evidence shows clearly that they could take such action if they chose to. As just one example of -- P01598, a 3 March 1993 Petkovic order which in part says: "Due to reasonable suspicion that he abused his official position as an HVO," general staff officer, "a Main Staff officer, abused the official stamp ... and tried forcibly to take someone else's apartment, I hereby order ... arrest this officer and investigate the above-mentioned circumstances." Wow. He can investigate the abuse of a stamp, but I wonder about investigating abuse of Muslims and expulsions from their homes, their imprisonment, the destruction of their property, their deportation. How about arresting and investigating people about those things rather than whether someone abused the use of an official stamp. The HVO government, including the Defence Department, invested substantial effort over a sustained course of time to enforce HVO mobilisation, that is, bringing Croat men into the HVO armed forces. It is clear from a review of the government records and meetings that this was an ongoing important issue. I refer the Chamber as an example to 4D00508, the minutes of an HVO government meeting on the 9th of October, 1993. Prlic chaired the meeting with Stojic, Praljak, and Petkovic all in attendance. Item 6 deals with the issue of mobilisation and dealing with, quote, "persons avoiding military obligation." "In addition to criminal sanctions, other measures shall also be taken against the persons avoiding military obligation. The following shall be done based on the exact list of persons avoiding their military obligation (and the Defence Administrations are required to create those lists immediately): "They shall be prevented from receiving personal papers and realising their rights resulting from dual citizenship in the Republic of Croatia; "The names of the people who are avoiding the military obligation shall be published in the media - radio press, et cetera; "Their families' shall lose their status of displaced persons or refugees; "Their families' electrical supply and telephone lines shall be cut and their privileges in receiving medical treatment, schooling, et cetera, revoked." Two days later, on 11 October 1993, Stojic issues an order to all military district courts and district military prosecutors, which is 4D01655: "1. All District Military Courts and District Military Prosecutors' Offices should give priority --" note that this is Stojic giving orders to Judges and Prosecutors as to what they should do: "All District Military Courts and Military Prosecutor's Offices should give priority to the cases related to the failure to respond to the call for general mobilisation and wilful abandonment of military units." Stojic then also ordered the assistance of the HVO military police in carrying these actions out. One can only wonder whether it might have made a difference of such severe and draconian actions as cutting off their families' displaced persons or refugee status and cutting off electrical supply -- their electrical supplies, blocking them from medical treatment, school, one can only wonder if such severe sanctions had been threatened or taken against people for the abuse of Muslims, for burning Muslim houses, for raping Muslim women, for expelling them, for destroying mosques, whether that might have made some difference, but there is no evidence of such a strong HVO position or such sustained efforts being made as those we can see that could be made and were made in connection with the mobilisation of Croat men into the armed forces. A few other examples. P03700. Slobodan Praljak order dated 25 July 1993 ordering HVO units from Kostajnica to Prozor: "Who does not carry out this order is to be disarmed, stripped of their HVO clothes, detained, and kept with no food or water until I come back." Fairly forceful action by an HVO commander. There again, I wonder if that might have been done in response to misconduct toward Muslims. 3D02798, a 12 October 1993 order by Mario Bradara, deputy commander of the HVO Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak, prescribing punishment for abandoning position on the confrontation line, prescribing that the unit -- that the violator will be put in front of the unit -- put in front of his unit, excuse me, and shot. The commander of his unit shall be proclaimed a traitor and also shot. Now, that may seem pretty extreme, but at least it was one person's view of the action to be taken in response to misconduct. As a final example, we have Mr. Petkovic's clear ability to take aggressive action to protect his friend and colleague, Mr. Rajic, Mr. Ivica Rajic, when he chose to do so. The Chamber will recall that Petkovic was fully capable of taking strong and decisive action when a group of HVO soldiers in the Kiseljak area mistreated Rajic first in mid-May 1993 and again in August 1993. On the first occasion, Petkovic suspended 12 HVO soldiers for their "maltreatment of Rajic." I'm just hesitating on a private session matter, Your Honours. I think in light of your prior ruling, I'll say this: When the misbehaviour of the HVO soldiers recurred in August 1993, Petkovic ordered an action to arrest nine or ten of the perpetrators, during which two of them were killed. There was evidence to the effect that what -- well, what did affect -- what affect did that action have on HVO command and control? "After the showdown with that criminal group you may say that the system of command was elevated to a somewhat higher level and that it was much easier to be in command of the units that I was in command of. Had a positive effect on military discipline." Mr. Petkovic could take those actions. He didn't take others. The failure by the HVO and the failure by these accused to take meaningful action in response to misconduct and crimes against Muslims wasn't a lack of means or a lack of opportunity but a lack of will. It was a lack of desire, being or becoming a decision not to do so, or stated differently, there was no point in punishing those who were in fact only carrying out HVO policy. And if that wasn't the case initially, that certainly came to be the case over time. Acquiescence in misconduct becomes ratification; ratification becomes approval; approval becomes encouragement; encouragement becomes instigation; and instigation becomes, in effect, ordering. Your Honours, that completes my part, at least this part, of the Prosecution's closing argument. Thank you.

One alternative, possibly, Mr. President, would be to take the break now for 20 minutes and then come back for the final hour and a half of the day, and then during the break we can make the transition.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. May it please the Court, I will be making the Prosecution's submissions on the case against General Slobodan Praljak. Not surprisingly, and like his co-accused, General Praljak denies responsibility for any single crime that occurred throughout the entire Herceg-Bosna territory throughout the entire HVO ABiH conflict. Where blame or responsibility is to be assigned, he assigns it to others, including at times, his co-accused. Praljak would have the Chamber believe that he had no real power or authority over subordinates and no knowledge of or ability to do anything about the widespread crimes directed against the Muslim people who were unfortunate enough to find themselves in Herceg-Bosna with Praljak during late 1992 and throughout 1993. The evidence, of course, paints a completely different picture, that of a strong-willed and charismatic commander and politician who achieved the highest political and military positions, assistant minister of defence for the Republic of Croatia, a member of the Croatian National Security Council, and trusted advisor to President Franjo Tudjman, a Major-General in the Croatian Army, and finally commander of the HVO Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Praljak rose to this level not based on his qualifications or military training, but rather based on, first, his fervent support of the Tudjman policy of re-establishing something akin to a Croatian Banovina in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and second, his willingness to do whatever it takes, including committing and condoning crimes linked to the forced movement of populations, to establish Herceg-Bosna in Bosnia-Herzegovina as an autonomous, permanent Croat-dominated territory. The evidence shows that at all times, whether exercising his de facto authority over HVO armed forces or his de jure authority after taking command of the HVO Main Staff on 24 July 1993, Praljak was in control and was fully informed of all significant events taking place throughout Herceg-Bosna, including the widespread crimes and persecution carried out by his subordinates in the HVO against the Muslim population. As HVO commander, Praljak moved frequently and easily throughout Herceg-Bosna, from Gornji Vakuf to Prozor to Mostar and down to the HVO forward command post headquarters in Citluk, ensuring that he was fully informed of events on the ground. He issued orders and directives to HVO subordinates from all of these locations, demonstrating his control over subordinate HVO units and their activities. When he was not in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Praljak was in Zagreb meeting with the Croatian leadership to discuss the Herceg-Bosna policy that he would then implement upon his return to Bosnia-Herzegovina. We know now that Praljak also travelled to Hungary and to Montenegro in October of 1992 with other accused in this case for meetings with Ratko Mladic, commander of the VRS Main Staff, hoping to enlist his support and collaboration in achieving the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina between the Croats and the Serbs. I will first address General Praljak's claims that there was no joint criminal enterprise and that, in any event, he did not participate in or contribute to a joint criminal enterprise. He claims this unequivocally from the very beginning of his brief in paragraphs 2 and 3. Your Honours, the evidence establishes beyond all doubt that Praljak, as well as his co-accused and other members of the Herceg-Bosna JCE, had as their goal the establishment of an autonomous, permanent, Croat-dominated entity within Bosnia-Herzegovina. When I say Croat-dominated, I mean that Praljak wanted to establish and maintain a Croat majority population in this territory which they called Herceg-Bosna. On the 29th of June, 2009, Praljak testified: "We were all hoping all that time that the leadership would finally understand that Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina wanted only one thing, and that was an autonomy in the area that could have been 17 or 18 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, an area in which they were an absolute or relative majority equal to anybody else." I believe Mr. Scott, my colleague, referred to this bit of testimony in his remarks yesterday when he was talking about two of the key things at that form part of the Prosecution's case, that of demographics and territory. Setting aside the fact that Praljak was in no position to decide what the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina wanted, Praljak's own words make two things clear: He and the accused wanted territory, and in that territory they wanted the majority of people to be Croats. Praljak testified on the 17th of August, 2009, transcript 43297, that this should be a permanent autonomous area for Croats, completely undermining Defence claims that Herceg-Bosna was simply a temporary entity intended to fill in for the Bosnia-Herzegovina government. In fact, Praljak's goal was identical to that of Prlic Defence witness Zoran Buntic, who testified as a Defence witness in this case as the former head of Herceg-Bosna's justice department. The Trial Chamber may recall his testimony in July of 2008, when he stated that he wanted an area in which Croatian people would be in the majority. He believed the Serbs and the Muslims should have their own different areas where they could be in the majority also. That's at page 30881 of the transcript. Praljak was, of course, fully aware this vision necessarily involved moving populations and that moving populations would require force and violence. While it is true that many parts of the so-called Herceg-Bosna had majority Croat populations, it's also true that many other parts had majority Muslim populations. Of course, in many municipalities, Croats and Muslims lived side by side and were mixed throughout the countryside, one of the defining attributes of Bosnia-Herzegovina itself at that time. We all know now that Mostar proclaimed to be the capital of Herceg-Bosna had been a place where Muslims and Croats intermarried in significant numbers, but Praljak was keenly aware that the Croat population was declining even in areas where they were in majority and that this trend was exacerbated by the fact that large numbers of Muslims, themselves expelled from the Serb-held territories, were arriving in areas claimed for Herceg-Bosna. P00524 is a transcript of a meeting that occurred on the 26th of September, 1992, at the presidential palace in Zagreb. President Tudjman, Slobodan Praljak, and others were present. At this meeting, Praljak raised his concern with Tudjman, observing that expulsion would be necessary in order to achieve a majority population. As he said: "As it seems now and due to the people settling on the territory from Travnik and below, I am afraid our chances will be bad at the moment when the war is over. There has been a great change in the ethnic structure. And to solve that with them by war, the civil, the international ... rights, et cetera, and it will be difficult in any form to expel those people from there, and without expelling those people, we will not have a majority there." Slobodan Praljak, on the 26th of September, 1992. Here Praljak clearly links forced population movement to the goal of achieving the desired Croat majority demographic. In paragraph 61 of his brief, Praljak tries to explain away this statement, claiming he was speaking in the conditional form, but his later actions prove otherwise. At the time of this conversation with President Tudjman in September of 1992, the Bosnian Serb armed forces had indeed driven thousands of non-Serbs from their homes and villages throughout much of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was, without doubt, the intended result of the Serbs' campaign to establish their own autonomous entity in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina where they, like the accused, like Croats, would be in the majority. In a post-war interview, Praljak indeed acknowledged that he and the Serbs shared this view, this vision, for Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is P09447. It's a clip that was played to General Praljak during his cross-examination in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] You had a communication problem regarding political and military co-operation with Izetbegovic and the Muslim army; on the other hand, the leadership in Zagreb fully supported you. How was this support manifested? Can you remember a specific meeting and action? Can you give us a story? "Praljak: There have been many meetings. The support consisted in -- well, once we realised what the intentions were -- the problem was that before the war, we were military allies with the Muslims, but the political ideas about a future state were completely opposite. To be honest, the Serb's political options for Bosnia-Herzegovina were closer to the Croats than that of the Muslims. Either we'll amend the constitution to provide for equal rights or we'll go separate ways."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: "To be honest, Serbs's political option for Bosnia-Herzegovina was closer to Croats than that of Muslims." That was indeed the case and is shown by the steps taken as early as October 1992 by General Praljak. P11376. Ten days after observing to President Tudjman that it would be necessary to expel the Muslims in order to achieve a majority, Praljak, in his capacity as assistant minister of defence for the Republic of Croatia, with the accused Prlic and Stojic, travelled to Pecu in Hungary where they held a secret meeting with General Ratko Mladic on the 5th of October, 1992, to discuss matters of common interest. The Trial Chamber is by now familiar with General Mladic's notes of this meeting at which Praljak distinctly described the objective: "The goal is the Banovina of 1939; if not, we'll continue the war." He makes the additional remark: "We shall not go further." That's at the bottom of the highlighted portion that the Trial Chamber sees. I'd like to step off of this exhibit for a moment, Mr. President. I'm going to come back to it but move to the next one, P00466, transcript of a meeting held not one month earlier, again in Zagreb, with President Tudjman. Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that in informing Mladic "we shall not go further," Praljak is repeating instructions issued by Tudjman during a meeting between Praljak, Tudjman, and Susak, only a few weeks earlier, on the 11th of September, when Tudjman made clear their military goal of holding the Banovina territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The HVO would not be involved in defending any territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina that fell outside of the 1939 Banovina which they believed was, in fact, Croatia itself. As Dr. Tudjman said: "Gentlemen, gentlemen, let's not orient, we have nothing to conquer, let's defend those Croatian ..." Praljak says: "Nowhere, Mr. President. It is impossible to pass further." Tudjman says: "And let's get ready to cleanse them out of Croatia. As I said, do not get involved in conquering Bosnia. "Praljak: No, Mr. President, believe me, the attacks have been stopped." Susak then says: "Nothing out of Banovina. We did not trespass, not one even metre." The evidence thus shows that in this meeting -- in his meeting on the 5th of October with Mladic, Praljak on behalf of Tudjman and Susak were assuring Mladic that the HVO would not challenge the Serbs for any territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina that fell outside of the Banovina. Now moving back to P011376, the Mladic diary excerpt from the 5th of October. It's worth noting - this is on page 10, I believe of the English version - that at this meeting Praljak and the other accused, notably Bruno Stojic, agreed that the HVO would repair the hydro-electric plant at Jajce in order to provide the Serbs with electricity, in exchange for which the Serbs would release water for use at other power plants. We see this in P11377, which is an order issued by General Mladic on the very next day after his meeting with Praljak, Stojic, and Prlic. On the 6th of October, Mladic issued this order, referring to his secret meeting with the leadership of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, saying: "... a meeting was held between the said leadership and the representatives of the Army of Republika Srpska. It was strictly confidential meeting and no information should be given about it. An agreement was reached regarding a cease-fire, the repair of the Jajce 2 hydro power plant, release of water ... and the exchange of prisoners." And then he issues this order in order to implement the procedures necessary to bring about the operation of the hydro-electric plant after its repair. P11380. Three weeks after the first meeting with Mladic in Hungary, Praljak, now with Petkovic, Prlic, and Stojic, met with Mladic again, this time in Njivice, Montenegro, on the 26th of October, 1992. Here Praljak reported that his side had adhered to the fundamental agreement and had reconnected the electric power plant near Jajce. He announced: "We're on a good path to compel Alija to divide Bosnia." Later in this meeting, he referred to the population movements he envisioned as part of the Herceg-Bosna plan, saying: "It is in our interest that the Muslims get their own canton so they have somewhere to move to." In having these discussions with none other than Ratko Mladic, the commander of the Bosnian Serb armed forces, in October of 1992, Praljak undoubtedly knew that the demographic engineering necessary to the establishment of an autonomous ethnic territory like Herceg-Bosna could not be accomplished without the violence of forced transfers and deportation, persecution, and destruction of property. The Serb experience made this clear, and all of the accused who were sitting that day with Ratko Mladic in Montenegro knew it. They knew the path they were on. 3D00482. Praljak again clearly expressed his views on establishment of the Banovina territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina as an autonomous Croat territory to a delegation of French officials during a meeting held in Zagreb on the 13th of January, 1993. While he reported that the Croats supported the territorial integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it's clear that to Praljak, this was only within the borders of a divided Bosnia-Herzegovina organised along separate ethnic lines. P01788. Praljak returned to the theme of population movements while chairing a meeting of HVO commanders in the Central Bosnia operative zone on April 2nd, 1993. His co-accused Valentin Coric was present together with HZ-HB vice-president Dario Kordic as well as Ignjac Kostroman. The Trial Chamber will recall that it was Mr. Kostroman, the gentleman from Central Bosnia, who had advocated that Herceg-Bosna should ultimately accede to become a part of Croatia in the meeting held with Tudjman in December of 1991. Meeting with the HVO commanders on the 2nd of April, 1993, Praljak shared his vision of the kind of society that Herceg-Bosna would be for non-Croats and others who failed to support the Croatian Defence council. As he said: "We shall ask for the HVO government and our provinces, those who choose not to submit can leave our territories." He continued: "Now we have got what we want, the homogenisation of our population continues. We can only fence off what is ours and build there our own space and our own state. It is all as clear as noon on a spring day." For Praljak, establishment of the state was only part of the goal. In all of his references to the establishment of Herceg-Bosna, we see from his own words that General Praljak consistently links this to demographics and population movements: "Croat majority," "expel them" to have a majority, "homogenisation of populations," those who don't accept the HVO governance can "leave our territories;" Muslims "moving into their own canton." We know, of course, that none of the population movements Praljak anticipated would take place on their own peacefully and voluntarily. In order to bring about the population movements and demographic changes he consistently refers to, Praljak and the other members of this joint criminal enterprise knew they would have to resort to crimes such as persecution, forcible transfer, deportation, and destruction. We know that as time went on, other large-scale crimes linked to this, for example, imprisonment of all the Muslim men in the Bosnia-Herzegovina territory, were ultimately resorted to. Your Honour, the Prosecution submits that the evidence firmly establishes beyond a reasonable doubt the criminal goals of the Herceg-Bosna joint criminal enterprise, and in particular, General Praljak's participation in it. Next I would like to address General Praljak's claim that he did not significantly contribute to the joint criminal enterprise as he states in paragraph 31 of his brief, and in order to illustrate one of his primary contributions to the Herceg-Bosna JCE, his role as conduit between the Croatian leadership in Zagreb and the HVO in Herceg-Bosna, I will discuss the role Praljak played in the events in Gornji Vakuf in January of 1993. This discussion will also clearly establish that Praljak wielded supreme military authority despite the fact that, as he readily points out, he did not have at that time an official title or rank within the HVO. Not surprisingly, the story of the HVO offensive and military success at Gornji Vakuf begins in Zagreb. As the Trial Chamber is fully aware, these events are linked to the ultimatum issued on the 15th of January, 1993, by Praljak's co-accused, Mr. Jadranko -- Dr. Jadranko Prlic, by which Prlic and the HVO demanded units of the ABiH found in the Vance-Owen Peace Plan cantons 3, 8, and 10, must either subordinate themselves to the HVO or withdraw from those areas altogether. In paragraph 63 of his brief, Praljak recalls his testimony in which he claimed that the text of the ultimatum was, in fact, agreed upon between Bosnia-Herzegovina President Izetbegovic and the Croatian leadership during meetings that took place in Zagreb during 13th and 14th of January, 1993. I'm referring now to his testimony at pages 40568 and 69, on the 21st of May, 2009. As Praljak said: "And when it comes to the drafting of the so-called ultimatum, I was involved in that together with some other people from the Muslim delegation, in the presence of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic." Praljak claimed that during the meetings in Zagreb, Izetbegovic and the Muslim delegation agreed that the ABiH would be subordinated to the HVO in Gornji Vakuf and elsewhere, or that the ABiH units would leave those territories altogether. Mr. President, Your Honours, the evidence does not support this claim, and in fact, it shows that Praljak lied to the Trial Chamber in giving this evidence. In claiming that he participated in drafting the ultimatum in Zagreb, Praljak led the Trial Chamber to believe that this alleged agreement with Izetbegovic was a written agreement. In fact, as we learn on cross-examination, Praljak conceded that it was not written, nor was anything signed by the alleged parties. On the 24th of August, 2009, at page 43701, he conceded it was not written and it was not signed, saying: "I didn't say that anyone signed it on behalf of the ... Muslims." I asked him: "So your evidence is that this was an oral agreement on the text?" He says: "Yes." Consider this, Your Honours: General Praljak wants the Trial Chamber to believe that President Izetbegovic reached an oral agreement with the leadership of the Republic of Croatia, providing either for the withdrawal of units of the army from the parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina falling within Vance-Owen cantons 3, 8, and 10, or for the subordination of the ABiH units to the HVO in those areas. Mr. President, I suggest that it is outlandish for anyone to make such a suggestion that such an agreement, if it were to exist, would be anything other than written and bearing signatures of all parties. Neither Praljak nor any other accused in this case has produced any such written agreement. Praljak's testimony about this alleged oral agreement on subordination or withdrawal of the ABiH to the HVO in Vance-Owen cantons 3, 8, and 10 is not worthy of your belief. P01158. This is a presidential transcript of the meeting held on the 15th of January, 1993, again in the presidential palace in Zagreb. President Izetbegovic was present at this meeting and they were discussing these matters. And the text of this transcript makes it clear that as of the 15th of January, when this meeting was held in Zagreb, there was no agreement between Izetbegovic and the Croatian leadership on this matter of alleged subordination or withdrawal. As President Izetbegovic said: "Mr. Boban said he understood from these papers that the armies -- that each army should withdraw to their territories. That's not how I understood the papers, and I don't know whether this was the intention of these documents. "Because I do not see that they define who has what territories, whose armies these are, you know. So I'm afraid what is now going on in Gornji Vakuf may have been caused by a misunderstanding of this item of these agreements. "I'm not sure I understood Mr. Boban correctly. But he seems to have understood that, say, now, that the Bosnian Army should withdraw from the region, from the Travnik province now, and the HVO should take it over completely. I did not understand these papers like this." Here, Izetbegovic makes clear that there was no agreement concerning the withdrawal or subordination of ABiH units in Gornji Vakuf or anywhere else. Based on Izetbegovic's comments at the 15 meeting, January, in Zagreb, how can Praljak seriously contend that Izetbegovic agreed to the text of the ultimatum that was issued on that day, the 15th of January, 1993? Izetbegovic's rejection of the Croatia HVO's self-serving interpretation of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan didn't stop Praljak. In an act that perfectly illustrates his role as the conduit or the bridge between Croatia's leadership and the leadership of Herceg-Bosna, Praljak travelled from Zagreb to Mostar on the 15th of January, personally handing the text of what became this ultimatum to Messrs. Prlic, Stojic, and General Petkovic there. The Trial Chamber is well acquainted with the evidence on what happened next, when the HVO HZ-HB government convened to adopt this text. Prlic issued the ultimatum, and it was then sent down the military chain of command, reaching Gornji Vakuf on that same day. This, of course, is not the end of General Praljak's involvement in and his contribution to the HVO's campaign in Gornji Vakuf and the eventual expulsion of the Muslim civilian population there. On the 21st of May, 2009, at page 40580 of the transcript, Praljak tells us that he went from Mostar and -- to Prozor. As he says, he arrived on the 16th of January: "In the evening, I heard everybody, the information, the arguments of the HVO officers, and I demanded that another round of talks be held with the BH Army in the presence of the English officers from UNPROFOR who were deployed there." Now, in a moment we'll see that's a reference to the British Battalion. This right away tells us, General Praljak tell us by his own admission, that he was immediately exercising his substantial de facto powers upon his arrival in Prozor, demanding another round of talks. At paragraph 235 of his brief, General Praljak tells us that he arrived in Prozor on the 16th of January. We know that he had meetings there with the operative zone commander Zeljko Siljeg. The evidence clearly establishes that upon his arrival in Prozor, Praljak exercised the greatest authority on behalf of the HVO armed forces, giving directions and orders to Siljeg that were immediately communicated in the form of demands and threats to the ABiH if they refused to accept the terms of the previous day's ultimatum and the text which Praljak had personally delivered from Zagreb. P01163 is the British Battalion UNPROFOR report of that day's events in Gornji Vakuf. This is at page 3 of the document, under item E. What it tells us is that even before he arrived in Prozor from Mostar, Praljak was issuing orders to the HVO Prozor command from Mostar. The British Battalion reported, on the 16th of January, that an HVO Colonel Andreivitich - who we say is actually Colonel Miro Andric, his name was misspelled by the British Battalion - read out a message from his commander, a general in Mostar. Since Petkovic was in Geneva at this time, the commander that Andric refers to is clearly Slobodan Praljak. The text of Praljak's message as read out by Andric and reported by the British Battalion states: "At the Geneva conference it was agreed that all provinces would be administered by the leading ethnic group, in this area the Croats." Praljak's message conveyed by Andric here, consistent with the text of the Prlic ultimatum, goes on to demand subordination of the ABiH to the HVO. Praljak's message also contained a threat that if the ABiH did not comply "in return the Croats and the HVO guarantee nothing will happen to the Muslim population, less those suspected of or accused of war crimes." The message continues by saying that if the ABiH agrees to the terms of this ultimate, "the Muslim population will be given full equality," as if Praljak reserved unto himself the authority to grant any one group full equality with any other group of inhabitants in this region. P01174. This is a report from the 17th of January by ABiH commander Dzemal Merdan, who was involved in the negotiations with the HVO on the ABiH side. His report independently corroborates the text of Praljak's demands as they were reported by the British Battalion. We know, of course, that the ABiH did not agree to the terms demanded by General Praljak and the HVO, and indeed, Praljak and the HVO made good on their threat. If Praljak had indicated nothing would happen to the Muslim population if the ABiH agreed to his terms, something indeed did happen to the Muslim population there in the days and weeks following the ABiH rejection of the ultimatum. The Muslim populations throughout Gornji Vakuf municipality were instead attacked on the 18th of January in Gornji Vakuf town and in a number of villages like Dusa, Hrasnica, Usricje, and Zdrimci, where they were driven from their homes, their property taken, and their homes destroyed. The men were either taken away or detained at a makeshift HVO detention centre at the furniture factory in Trnovaca, where they were beaten and abused. The women and children were rounded up and crammed into a few empty houses, where they endured harsh conditions and mistreatment by the HVO for weeks before they were expelled in the ABiH territory. P01162. Getting back to the 16th of January when Praljak did arrive in Prozor, he ratcheted up the rhetoric of his demands as soon as he arrived. At 8.00 that evening, the HVO operative zone commander Siljeg sent this report to the HVO Main Staff headquarters in Mostar, reporting on the negotiations with the ABiH. The bottom of page 2, Siljeg states: "Tonight, at Gornji Vakuf, Colonel Siljeg and Colonel Andric negotiated with BH Army representatives. There were no results. Unless there is an agreement, Gornji Vakuf southern strongholds (Uzricje, Duse, mount Mackovac) will be taken and our line strengthened." He then adds: "General Praljak sent them a message that they will be annihilated if they do not accept the decisions of the HZ-HB." Throughout his testimony and throughout his brief General Praljak has assured the Trial Chamber that, in fact, he was only sent to Gornji Vakuf with the mission of calming the situation down, calming the situation there. Let's take a look and see who, in fact, was trying to calm the situation. P01168. On the 16th of January, ABiH Commander Sefer Halilovic sent this order from Sarajevo to all of his commands regarding the HVO ultimatum issued on the previous day. Item 3 orders them to take measures to "realise further co-operation with the HVO and to prevent any conflicts between HVO and the BiH Army. Extreme behaviour of some individuals and groups within BH Army towards members of the HVO are to be prevented." Item 4: "Estimate current situation and possible conflict situations in relation to HVO HZ-HB decisions and make a plan of measures for preventing them." However, General Praljak's personal involvement in demanding the subordination or withdrawal of the ABiH units from Gornji Vakuf and elsewhere made the conflict there inevitable. After the ABiH rejected the HVO ultimatum and the demands issued by Praljak through Siljeg and Andric, Praljak continued to exercise his de facto HVO authority to support the HVO military operations in Gornji Vakuf. P01202. On the 18th of January, on the day of the attack, Praljak issued this order from Prozor to the HVO south-east operative zone, directing that certain assets be sent "due to the complicated situation in Gornji Vakuf ... and the need to engage in combat activity." In response to a question from Judge Antonetti, Praljak testified that although he did not sign this order personally, he had said, "Okay. Fine. Use my authority, and we'll ask for those three pieces to be returned." That's at page 41882 of the transcript. Praljak continued to direct and participate in HVO activities affecting Gornji Vakuf in the following days. P01293. At this time, General Petkovic was in Geneva taking part in the negotiations there. On what appears to be or is at least the 20th or 21st of January, 1993, the document itself is not dated, Petkovic issues this order from Geneva on a cease-fire, and further directing in item 3 that: "Colonel Siljeg is to report directly --" excuse me. "Colonel Siljeg is to report urgently to Brada in Mostar and send a report on the situation in Gornji Vakuf directly." In his testimony, Praljak acknowledged that Brada was a reference to him. That's at page 44117. P01277. Siljeg clearly complied with Petkovic's order and continued to take orders from Praljak, reporting on 23 January to the Defence Department, as well as the HVO Main Staff, on the 23rd of January: "I issued necessary orders that were in the spirit of the orders issued by 'Brada ' and they were carried out." On the same day that Siljeg sent this report down to the HVO Defence Department and Main Staff, the HVO continued to engage in ethnic cleansing of the civilian Muslim population in Gornji Vakuf. In its report of 23 January, in item 3, this is P01278, the British Battalion noted the HVO rocket attack on the village of Bistrica where houses in the village were reported to be burning fiercely. The report notes the British Battalion Cheshire unit in the area was, quote, "keen to stress that this was most definitely ethnic cleansing by Croats on a Muslim village." Your Honours, in this evidence on the lead-up in the events occurring in Gornji Vakuf in January 1993, the Prosecution submits that one finds overwhelming proof of Praljak's contribution to the Herceg-Bosna JCE and its goal of carving out an autonomous Croatian entity there at the expense of the Muslim population. We also see the supreme de facto authority Praljak exercised in directing and controlling HVO communications with the ABiH side, insisting on implementation of the ultimatum, threatening annihilation in the event of refusal, and directing that additional military assets be transferred to the area when the HVO resort to force became necessary to achieve its goals. There is yet another important point to make based on Praljak's involvement in the events in Gornji Vakuf. In his brief, Praljak denies that the HVO-ABiH conflict was an international armed conflict, claiming that many of the crimes alleged were bottom-up events, only tangentially related to the wider conflict. The Trial Chamber can reject this assertion based solely on Praljak's role and the positions he held within the Croatian government and the Croatian military before even taking command of the HVO Main Staff in July of 1993. For example, the leading role that Praljak played in Gornji Vakuf compels the Trial Chamber to find a nexus between the crimes committed there and international armed conflict. The Prosecution brief, as well as annex material submitted with it, fully demonstrates the existence of an international armed conflict at all times of relevance in this case based on the overall control that Croatia in its leadership exercised over the HVO and the direct and active participation of Croatian Army units, personnel, and equipment fighting on the side of the HVO against the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina inside Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, I would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to paragraphs 75 and 76 of the Prosecution brief in which we identify an additional basis on which to find international armed conflict based upon the language of the Appeals Chamber judgement in the Tadic case. In Tadic, the Appeals Chamber states: "International law renders any state responsible for acts in breach of international law performed (i) by individuals having the formal status of organs of a state (and this occurs even when these organs act ultra vires or contra legem) or (ii) by individuals who make up organised groups subject to the State's control." The Tadic judgement thus refers to state responsibility for the acts of individuals having the formal status of organs of the state. Until shortly before taking command of the HVO Main Staff in July of 1993, General Praljak was an assistant minister of defence of the neighbouring Republic of Croatia. He was a major-general in its army. He was a member of Croatia's National Security Council. P01458. This decision of Mr. Sarinic and the Croatian Ministry of Defence, dated the 10th of February, 1993, tells us that General Praljak was indeed on the payroll of the Croatian Ministry of Defence in January of 1993, at the same time that he was down in Gornji Vakuf directing Siljeg, Andric, and the HVO in their negotiations with the ABiH and issuing threats on annihilation, issuing orders on the movement of military equipment into the region. When he testified, Praljak agreed that his salary was paid by Croatia at all times during 1993, even after he took command of the HVO Main Staff. That's at page 42993. Mr. President, Your Honours, there is no doubt that Praljak was indeed a de jure organ of the State of Croatia in Bosnia-Herzegovina until July 1993, when he resigned his positions as a Croatian official to take up his position as commander of the HVO Main Staff. After the 24th of July, 1993, he remained on Croatia's payroll and continued to confer with Tudjman and Susak, implementing Croatia's Herceg-Bosna policy in Bosnia-Herzegovina. On page 43001 of the transcript, there is a highly interesting and relevant exchange that occurred between the two of us, myself and General Praljak, during his cross-examination. I put it to him: "But at all times you were down in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and your job was to see to it that President Tudjman's policies were implemented and carried out; isn't that true? He was your boss. At all times, you were answerable to him, and it was your job to implement his policy; correct? "A. No. I was implementing the policies of the Croatian state. I wasn't there on a permanent basis. I was there at very precise points in time ..." There's no question that as he told us himself, General Praljak was in Bosnia-Herzegovina implementing the policies of Croatia, and that has a huge impact on the question of international armed conflict even apart from the other issues and the points, which have amply been proven as well, regarding the HVO being a group under the overall control of the Croatian leadership or the direct participation of units and personnel and equipment of the Croatian Army in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'd like to now turn to some issues and some discussion on command and control, General Praljak's effective command and control, his ability to impose discipline, disciplinary measures, and his powers to stop the many crimes that were being committed against the Bosnian Muslim populations throughout the areas that were under HVO control. Throughout his brief, General Praljak claims repeatedly that he was either not responsible for or could not control subordinate members of the HVO who committed crimes. He frames this issue largely as one of command responsibility under Article 7(3) of the Statute, but in fact, those issues are also directly linked to his criminal responsibility under Article 7(1). For example, Praljak claims he did not contribute to the JCE. In fact, his permissive and accepting attitude in regard to the numerous crimes committed by his HVO subordinates, the command climate he established by abandoning his obligation to protect civilians was itself a very substantial contribution to the achievement of the Herceg-Bosna JCE. Issues of responsibility and the Praljak command climate also bear directly on his liability under other parts of Article 7(1), such as ordering, instigating, and aiding and abetting the widespread criminal conduct of the HVO armed forces. General Praljak denies having effective control over subordinates unless he was physically present with them. He claims he was powerless to punish perpetrators of crimes that weren't committed in his presence. He denies responsibility for the conduct of HVO soldiers who were not engaged in specific combat activities on the front line. He denies responsibility for any crime that occurred when he was not commander of the HVO Main Staff. He denies having any responsibility for the HVO prison camps and detention facilities or for the conditions and mistreatment of prisoners there. As an accused in this Tribunal, and more importantly as a commander of soldiers in the field who controlled the areas in which large numbers of civilians were found, Praljak does not get to choose between which aspects of effective command and control apply to him and which do not. He, without doubt, exercised effective control over his men. As he told you himself, he led them in battle frequently in Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, Boksevica, and elsewhere. He regained lost territory. He rallied the troops. As General Praljak acknowledges in his brief, he did have effective command and control of his subordinates when he was physically present with them in the field in connection with their combat taskings. He testified several times about taking direct operational control over military police units to deploy them in combat. He issued many orders, and those orders were carried out. Let's look briefly at Exhibits P04640 and 4645. In 4640, we see on the 30th of August, General Praljak issues an order as commander of the Main Staff, from the Citluk headquarters to the south of Mostar, directing that the commander of an Independent Battalion submit a report to him as to why a certain order was not carried out. He directed, that is, Praljak directed, in item 2, that this order was to be carried out immediately and unconditionally. We find in P04645 that on the very next day, the 31st of August, 1993, the commander at issue did, indeed, submit a written statement to Praljak, as directed, acknowledging that the order had not been carried out, but informing Praljak that arrangements were made for this battalion to discharge its duties on the following day. The question of command and control we submit, Mr. President and Your Honours, is not seriously in question. Praljak did indeed possess and exercise effective command and control over his subordinates. Had Praljak shown himself to be unable to exercise effective command and control over HVO subordinates prior to 24 July 1993, no one would have considered appointing to him to the position of commander of the HVO Main Staff at that time. He was offered that position precisely because he was effective. What Praljak is really claiming is that he didn't have command and control over his soldiers when they were committing crimes against Muslim civilians who were living in areas under HVO control. In other words, for successful combat operations of the HVO, General Praljak happily takes credit, but when blame is to be assigned for crimes committed by his subordinates, Praljak conveniently asserts that he was powerless to do anything about. The fact is, apart from his empty words while testifying in this case, there is no evidence that Praljak attempted to impose his will on subordinates to stop them from committing crimes against the Muslim population or to punish subordinates for having done so. For purposes of his command responsibility under Article 7(3), the question, simply put, is whether Praljak had the material ability to take measures that would stop the crimes from happening, to prevent the perpetrators from committing more crimes or to punish or bring about the punishment of perpetrators. The answer is, of course, Slobodan Praljak, assistant minister of defence for the Republic of Croatia, a Major-General in that army, and as commander of the HVO Main Staff did indeed have the material ability to do something about the crimes that were happening all around him. Did he make any genuine effort to do so? The answer is no. P03829. Shortly after taking command of the HVO Main Staff on the 30th of July, 1993, General Praljak demanded that Mr. Coric, chief of the Military Police Administration, provide him with the names of some military police officers who'd been involved in beating up the drivers of a convoy from Germany. We don't know where the convoy was destined to go or who its beneficiaries would be, but we surely know that Praljak had no hesitation on this occasion in demanding from the chief of the Military Police Administration identification of the individuals involved. He expressly directed that those individuals were to be sent to him. P03700. I believe this is an order my colleague Mr. Scott referred to in his submissions earlier today. This is another Praljak order. Item number 2: "Who does not carry out this order is to be disarmed, stripped off from the HVO clothes, detained ... kept with no food or water until I come back." P03706, 25th of July, 1993. In an order to his operative zone Commander Siljeg personally: "Failure to carry out the received order until 1700 hours on 26 July 1993 would mean: "1. That the said commanders, as the most responsible persons, will be replaced and criminal proceedings instituted against them." P03773. Another example of Praljak's willingness to threaten serious consequences for misconduct or failing to carry out orders is found in this document. Here he threatens that commanders who fail to carry out this order shall be held to account according to the HZ-HB Criminal Code. As the Appeals Chamber indicated in paragraph 63 of its judgement in the Halilovic case, for purposes of command responsibility under Article 7(3), the question is: Did the accused genuinely try to prevent or punish crimes by taking measures that fell within his material powers? These examples that I've just shown in which Praljak demanded the identity of perpetrators, for example, or threatened criminal proceedings under the criminal law, these were all well within his sphere of competence. He very clearly believed that issuing orders and directives like this was within his material powers as commander of the HVO. However, there is not one example of Praljak ever issuing any order, complaint, or threat like these against, for example, perpetrators of the expulsion of Muslims from West Mostar throughout the many months that he was commander the Main Staff and as well as the weeks and months before that, or the campaign of terror directed again the Muslim population in Prozor throughout 1993, a place where he spent a lot of his time after taking command of the HVO Main Staff. Did he ever issue any orders or strongly-worded communications of any kind like this in order to bring an end to the forced labour? We'll talk about that labour later, but the answer is he did not. He knew all of these crimes were occurring. Did Praljak ever demand that Coric or anyone else provide him with the names of the perpetrators of any of these crimes in West Mostar, Prozor or elsewhere? There is no question that Praljak had the material ability and the authority to issue such a command, and in doing so, he would have made it clear that he would not tolerate such conduct. He never exercised this authority. He never even tried. He never even tried. With the exception of Stupni Do, there is no evidence that Praljak ever even ordered disciplinary measures against HVO soldiers who committed crimes against Muslims or that he ordered an investigation of any of the widespread crimes that occurred either prior to or after he became commander of the HVO Main Staff. You might be stripped of your uniform for failing to follow orders but not for driving hundreds of Muslim civilians from their homes. Although Praljak claims he wasn't responsible for HVO crimes committed away from the front line or that he couldn't do anything about crimes not committed in his presence, the truth is that he turned a blind eye to the crimes committed by HVO soldiers when they weren't at the front line. As he made very clear during his testimony, Praljak only cared about winning the war, winning the battle at hand. He claimed, for example, that he could not discipline soldiers because this would result in their removal from the front line. Page 41035 of the transcript from the 2nd of June, 1992. General Praljak told us: "And on the assumption that you did have the power and authority to put 300 soldiers in prison, into some kind of prison, you still wouldn't have another 300 soldiers to take up their positions at the front lines." So it wasn't a problem that could be solved within the frameworks of the resources that you had and the way in which we acted and in which we existed. Mr. President and Your Honours, I submit to you that it wouldn't have required putting 300 soldiers in gaol. Strong and decisive measures against a smaller number would have certainly sent the signal and would have had, as General Pringle tells us, a profound effect on the command climate that existed under Praljak's command. The Trial Chamber will recall that Praljak made a conscious decision to subject the civilian population to even more crime and terror by using police, both military and civilian, in combat operations. Page 43991 of the transcript. I'm sure the Trial Chamber will recall these passages. Here on cross-examination, General Praljak affirmed his earlier testimony on the direct in which he had said: "Such a use of the military police will significantly decrease the ability of the military police to perform their tasks, their normal tasks, and that for that reason there will be an increase in the rate of general crime, and there will also be a decrease in the number of those who will be arrested for those crimes." On the 27th of August, 2009, we return to this theme at page 43997 of the transcript, with Judge Trechsel intervening with the following question asking for clarification from General Praljak on this: "You took that in account. You were aware of it, and your point is that this was a case of necessity; that is to say, the situation was so tense and the end of fighting the enemy justified the means of drawing away a police force, which exposed civilians to a greater risk of crime. Have I understood that correctly?" General Praljak says: "Correct. Unfortunately, that's how it was. You have understood my answer correctly." Moving down a number of lines he says: "The military situation was such that it was necessary to have a part of the military police force engaged in battle." P04177. The effect, the impact on the ground of General Praljak's decision to abandon protection of the civilian population is shown graphically in this report from the 14th of August, 1993, of a SIS officer in Prozor. He describes the horrific situation facing the Muslim population there at the time when Praljak himself was personally in Prozor. The report notes: "The arrival of soldiers and civilians into the municipality has caused an increase in crime, prostitution, removal of Muslims from prison and their liquidation, the extortion of gold, money, other valuables ... "Every day women and girls are taken out from the collection centres of Podgrade, Lapsunj, and Duge, which are not secure ..." We will talk more in my submissions about Mr. Coric, but it was, in fact, a primary role and responsibility of military police to provide security in the HVO detention centres. " ... collection centres are not secure and taken to houses where they are raped, abused, humiliated. For example, naked women have to serve them. They are beaten until they agree to have sex, and some have their hair shaven off." Next page. After the reference to men going to the Muslim houses and the mistreatment and abuse that takes place there, he reports: "This has all been happening systematically for a considerable time now, even though we informed the HVO President Mijo Jozic, the brigade commander, and the commanders of the military and civilian police of this in writing." Moving on to the next page. Whereas General Praljak, what's he doing in the midst of all this terror reigning in Prozor? At the bottom of the page: "The civilian police are unable to cope with all this and recently they have been mostly in the field under the command of General Slobodan Praljak." The evidence proves that General Praljak concluded it would undermine the HVO's ability to win the war if he took steps to punish or discipline HVO soldiers committing crimes against Muslim civilians and so he did nothing. Distilled down to its essence, as he indicated in responding to Judge Trechsel's question, General Praljak's position was that military necessity, i.e., winning the war, justified exposing the civilian population to the kind of widespread crime, persecution, and terror that we see in this SIS report and in other places as well, such as West Mostar. However, as we note in our brief, military necessity is never justification for crime. A military commander cannot simply disregard the law and turn a blind eye to crimes by his subordinates because that's what he needs to do to win the war. Of course, the crimes condoned by General Praljak were a necessary part of driving the Muslim population out of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it is here, Mr. President and Your Honours, that the consequences of General Praljak's conscious decision not to prevent or punish crimes, the consequences of that reach across from Article 7(3) to Article 7(1) of the Statute. Given Praljak's fervent support for the establishment of a Croat-dominated Herceg-Bosna, a goal that necessarily involved crimes linked to forced population movements, Praljak's acceptance of widespread criminal conduct on the part of his subordinates itself constitutes a significant, indeed a tremendous contribution to the Herceg-Bosna JCE. Joint criminal enterprise is, of course, a form of committing under Article 7(1). We don't have to speculate about what sort of -- excuse me -- what sort of command climate would exist when the highest-ranking commander denies all responsibility for conduct of his subordinates when they are out of his sight and when he knowingly exposes the civilian population to increased crime by condoning crime and deploying military and civilian police in combat operations. The Trial Chamber need only read the reports of the evidence taking place -- of the events taking place in Prozor, Mostar, and throughout Western Herzegovina and elsewhere, all of HVO-controlled territory, to see the kind of terror, expulsion, and destruction that flourish in such a climate. This is the climate that Slobodan Praljak nurtured. Win the war at all cost, the end justifies the means. Condone and turned a blind eye to crimes by subordinates so long as they continue to return to their front line positions the next day to fight for Herceg-Bosna. Coming from the supreme commander of the HVO, this was a supreme contribution to the joint criminal enterprise. Tribunal jurisprudence in such cases as Galic and others makes clear that the repeated and consistent failure to prevent crimes or to take reasonable and necessary measures against perpetrators can itself lead to the conclusion that such crimes were intended and indeed ordered under Article 7(1). We know also that by repeatedly tolerating crimes, the acts and omissions of a senior commander may constitute instigation of crimes when he has created an environment permissive of criminal behaviour. These legal principles apply directly in the case of General Praljak and his total unwillingness to exercise any form of control or discipline over his subordinates to deal with the widespread crimes of deportation, eviction, looting and appropriation, destruction of property directed against the Muslim civilian populations throughout the areas under HVO control. The evidence shows that he, in fact, accepted these crimes as necessary to that objective. The objective of, in his words, "fencing off what is ours and creating there our own State." Mr. President, I submit to you that it's all as clear as noon on a spring day. This is a good time for me to break, Mr. President.
